newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF unshakeably committed to stable franc - Trichet.
newsitem.headline: BoF unshakeably committed to stable franc - Trichet.

text.p: Bank of France governor Jean-Claude Trichet said on Friday the Bank was unshakeably committed to the stability of the franc and dismissed calls from within the Bank for faster rate cuts as purely personal opinions.

"The monetary policy council has only one voice as a collegiate. It is the voice of its president, governor, and spokesman, as is the case for all the other major independent central banks in the world," Trichet said in a statement.

"In Paris, as in Frankfurt, as in Washington, the members of the council speak in a personal capacity. They clearly have the right to do so within the limits of our independent status, given our appreciation of the overriding interest which the law requires of us, that is to defend monetary stability," he said.
Trichet made the written statement in response to a request for comment on a renewed debate in France on the merits of its decade-long policy of keeping the franc stable against the mark.

"The Bank of France is unshakeably committed to the stability of the franc in the group of the most credible European currencies, which comprise in particular the franc, the mark, the guilder, the Belgian franc, the Danish crown and the Austrian schilling," Trichet said.

"Naturally, nothing could justify a depreciation of the franc versus the other most credible currencies of the exchange rate mechanism, with a French economy which will have the third largest current account surplus in the world this year," he said.

Shortly afterwards Finance Minister Jean Arthuis also issued his own statement repeating the government was "very firmly" attached to the stability of the franc. This was the necessary condition for low interest rates, needed for growth and jobs.

The debate on France's strong franc policy, which until now politicians have only questioned privately, burst into the open last week after ex-president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a sharp depreciation in the franc to revive growth.

Two members of the nine-member monetary policy, in an unusually public airing of doubts from the central bank's inner sanctum, then this week suggested the Bank could move faster on easing interest rates.

Though the two are believed to be in a minority, their comments were given added bite by the fact that the mandates of two others council members -- ex-journalist Jean Boissonnat and banker Bruno de Maulde -- are coming up for renewal.

Markets are watching very closely the government's decision on this for any sign President Jacques Chirac may be preparing for a change of policy in the face of rising unemployment and public discontent.
Trichet in his statement made a point of stating that pursuit of exchange rate stability was backed by Chirac and his Prime Minister Alain Juppe.

"This exchange rate stability is part of the monetary policy council's policy. It is enshrined in the European policy of the President of the Republic and the Prime Minister and the strategic goal of Economic and Monetary Union decided by the President," he said.
